claims.text: Sustained high-temperature oxidation resistance and material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by their ability to form and maintain a continuous, self-healing protective oxide scale.
Reactive elements such as Al or Cr segregate to alloy surfaces and grain boundaries during high-temperature exposure.
Surface- and grain-boundary-segregated Al or Cr preferentially oxidizes to form dense, adherent Al2O3 or Cr2O3.
Severe lattice distortion in multiprincipal-element alloys slows oxygen diffusion and impedes internal oxidation.
The initial as-cast alloy is an equiatomic or near-equiatomic disordered solid solution.
The initial as-cast alloy has a uniform grain structure and minimal secondary phases.
Increasing Al or Cr content facilitates formation of a continuous and adherent surface oxide layer.
Al2O3 or Cr2O3 forms a dense, slow-growing protective scale that retards further oxygen ingress.
Lattice distortion disrupts fast diffusion pathways and reduces surface and internal oxidation.
Protective oxide formation together with reduced oxygen diffusion preserves alloy microstructural integrity.
Protective oxide formation together with reduced oxygen diffusion delays degradation of mechanical properties.
An alloy with elevated reactive-element content will form a more continuous, adherent, and slow-growing oxide scale than a comparable alloy with lower reactive-element content.
Elevated reactive-element content will produce lower oxidation weight-gain rates than the lower-content baseline.
Elevated reactive-element content will reduce surface and subsurface degradation relative to the lower-content baseline.
The protective behavior will reduce oxide spallation and cracking during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
A lower-reactive-element baseline is expected to form a more discontinuous or less adherent oxide scale.
A lower-reactive-element baseline is expected to oxidize faster and lose material properties more rapidly under identical conditions.
The proposed governing behavior applies in air or oxygen-rich atmospheres between 1000 and 1200 degrees Celsius.
Water vapor, chloride ions, or substantially different oxygen partial pressure may invalidate the proposed behavior.
At sufficiently long durations, scale spallation or cyclic-oxidation mechanisms may dominate over the proposed protective behavior.
